title: Looking Through Energy Price Shocks When Inflation Is High: Evidence from a Euro Area Panel
content: Should a central bank still look through energy price shocks when inflation is already high? We address the question with state-dependent local projections on a monthly panel of the twenty euro area countries from 2001 to 2025, using innovations in euro-denominated oil and natural gas prices. A price-setting framework with state-dependent price adjustment, real wage resistance and limited attention delivers three testable predictions. The evidence supports the look-through prin- ciple in three respects. Average second-round effects are small: a 10 per cent oil price innovation raises core prices by 0.13 per cent after one year. Beyond the month of the shock, transmission from commodity prices to consumer energy prices does not depend on the inflation regime. Out- side two episodes, pass-through to core prices when inflation exceeds 4 per cent is no larger than at low inflation. State dependence is present in household expectations, which respond immedi- ately to gas price innovations only when inflation is high, a result that holds when any single year is excluded. In the full sample, oil pass-through to core prices is 0.31 per cent in the high-inflation regime against 0.07 per cent otherwise, and we show that this difference originates in 2008 and 2022, when energy prices moved together with large aggregate disturbances. Gas shocks transmit more slowly and more persistently than oil shocks. The results indicate that the case for respond- ing more forcefully to energy shocks at high inflation rests on expectations and on the coincidence of shocks, and less on a mechanical rise in pass-through.
